{{< include _score-kit.qmd >}}

Transposing parts look like a puzzle invented to annoy conductors. They are actually a solution, and
each one solved a real problem for players. Knowing the history also explains why an 1800 symphony asks
for "horns in E♭" in one movement and "horns in C" in the next.

## 1. Natural horns and trumpets

Before valves, a horn or trumpet was a single long tube. It could play only the notes of **one harmonic
series**: the fundamental and its overtones. On a tube built for C that means C, G, C, E, G, B♭, C, D,
E… and nothing in between, except what horn players could bend with a hand in the bell (**hand-stopping**,
which also changes the tone).

To play in another key, the player changed the length of the tube by fitting a **crook**, an extra coil of
tubing. A longer crook gave a lower series. Crooks were in common use by about 1740, and a horn player
carried a set: B♭ alto, A, G, F, E, E♭, D, C, B♭ basso and more.

## 2. Why the part stayed in C

Whatever crook was fitted, the player's lips worked the same way: the third harmonic felt like the third
harmonic. So composers wrote the part **as if the horn were in C**, and named the crook: "Corno in E♭".
The player fitted the E♭ crook and read the same written notes with the same feel; the instrument did the
transposing. Many such parts have **no key signature**: the few notes needed outside the harmonic series
were written in with accidentals.

That is why the horn and trumpet parts of Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms are "in" so many keys,
sometimes changing between movements while the player swapped crooks.

## 3. Valves, and the horn in F

Valves (Heinrich Stölzel applied them to the horn in 1814) let one instrument switch tube length
instantly, so one horn could play every note. Players settled on the horn in F, and later the
double horn in F and B♭, but composers kept writing for horn in E, D, E♭ well into the century. Today's
players still meet all of them, and read them on the F horn by transposing at sight.

## 4. Reading horn parts on the F horn

Work out the distance from F to the part's key, and move every written note by that much:

| Part says horn in | Read each written note | Example: written C becomes |
|---|---|---|
| B♭ alto | up a perfect 4th | F |
| A | up a major 3rd | E |
| A♭ | up a minor 3rd | E♭ |
| G | up a major 2nd | D |
| **F** | **as written** | C |
| E | down a minor 2nd | B |
| E♭ | down a major 2nd | B♭ |
| D | down a minor 3rd | A |
| D♭ | down a major 3rd | A♭ |
| C (basso) | down a perfect 4th | G |
| B♭ basso | down a perfect 5th | F |

F-horn player reads them:

## 5. Trumpets in every key

Trumpet parts went through the same history: natural trumpets in D, E♭, F and others, with parts written in
C. Modern players read them on a B♭ or C trumpet, or pick a smaller trumpet (D, E♭, piccolo) for high
Baroque parts. On a B♭ trumpet: a part in C reads up a major 2nd, in D up a major 3rd, in E♭ up a perfect 4th.
Careful with old trumpet parts "in F": they sound a 4th *above* written, unlike the horn in F.

<div class="sq" data-quiz="sound" data-only="tpt"></div>

## 6. Clarinets in B♭ and A

Early clarinets had few keys and could not play chromatically, so they were limited to keys close to their
own. Builders made clarinets in several keys, and the composer chose the one that made the part easy:
a concert-sharp key went to the A clarinet, a flat key to the B♭. Keywork improved, the C clarinet faded,
but remote keys stayed awkward, so orchestral clarinettists still keep a B♭ and an A clarinet side by side
and parts still switch between them ("muta in A", change to A).

## 7. One fingering for a whole family

Adolphe Sax patented the saxophone in 1846, as families in E♭/B♭ and C/F. Every size uses the same
fingering, so a written note means the same finger pattern on soprano, alto, tenor or baritone. Writing them
as transposing instruments lets a player switch sizes without relearning anything. The E♭/B♭ family won.

British brass bands took the idea furthest: every instrument except the bass trombone reads treble clef as a
transposing instrument, so a player can move from cornet to tenor horn to euphonium to bass with the same
fingerings for the same written notes.

## 8. Octave transpositions: just ledger lines

The last reason is the simplest. Piccolo, glockenspiel, double bass and guitar would spend their lives on
ledger lines at sounding pitch, so their parts are moved by whole octaves to sit on the staff.
